A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same StreamV2V research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 67 DAVIS video-prompt pairs, a human preference study, StreamV2V runtime measurements and ablations on 18 in-house videos.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds qualitative demonstrations of continuous text-to-image generation and long-video translation.

M1.justification: Extended self-attention, feature fusion and dynamic feature-bank merging remain unchanged. Sections 4.2–4.3 explain existing masking and merging operations more explicitly; the continuous-generation demonstration does not specify a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v2 adds limited qualitative coverage of continuous text-to-image generation with evolving prompts (Section 5.5) and explicitly demonstrates translation beyond 1000 frames (Appendix A.4). The DAVIS evaluation, webcam/drawing applications and in-house video coverage are retained.

E2.justification: The five main V2V comparators remain StreamDiffusion, CoDeF, Rerender, TokenFlow and FlowVid. v2 additionally reports a continuous-generation comparison against per-frame LCM without a feature bank (Figure 9). Live2Diff is discussed but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The added demonstrations introduce comparisons across successively extended prompts and long-video inspection at frames 0, 250, 450, 650 and 1000. Existing benchmark metrics, user-study procedures, default inference settings and the 120-frame runtime benchmark remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figure 9 tests whether the feature bank stabilizes generation under small prompt changes; Figure 15 adds a qualitative check of consistency over a long sequence. Existing component, bank-size, fusion-position and denoising-step analyses are retained, including the denoising analysis moved into Appendix A.3.

E5.justification: Section 5.3.3 newly discloses ten StreamV2V timing runs, discarding the two highest and two lowest measurements and averaging six. This establishes additional reporting, not an increase over a known earlier run count. The user-study participant counts and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting already existed and remain unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds qualitative results showing smoother transitions during prompt entry and sustained face/style appearance in a long video. Existing numerical results are unchanged, including StreamV2V's 96.58 CLIP score, 102.99 warp error, nine-second runtime and user-preference statistics.

T1.justification: The attention and fusion equations remain unchanged. v2 writes out standard cosine-similarity and averaging formulas for operations already described in v1; this adds explanation rather than new mathematical reasoning. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the novelty claim from the first approach to one of the first approaches for real-time streaming V2V translation. The abstract and conclusion retain the same central feature-bank, training-free operation, efficiency and consistency claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit application guidance favoring StreamV2V for speed-critical webcam/drawing tasks and slower methods such as FlowVid for short-content quality. Appendix A.5 frames the user study as a first-impression comparison, and Section 5.5 discusses applicability beyond V2V. Existing failure cases and limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the fusion-mask threshold of 0.9 and explains the matching/masking procedure, identifies the retained DAVIS selection as trainval 2017, and adds software-source references for Tiny Autoencoder and TensorRT. These clarify documentation without establishing changed underlying implementations or data splits.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds concurrent Live2Diff and distinguishes StreamV2V's training-free approach from its video fine-tuning. Tiny Autoencoder and TensorRT references are also added. The remaining research positioning is substantially retained; conversion to author-date citations is stylistic.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted prose corrections and expands the streaming motivation, masking/merging explanations and user-study discussion. It inserts Section 5.5 and folds the former denoising-step appendix subsection into A.3. The overall narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the continuous-generation and long-video image grids, clarifies labels in Figure 3, and changes title/heading typography and page layout. Existing figures and tables are retained with relocation and renumbering, including the user-study statistics table moving to the final page.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility through the explicit fusion threshold and timing aggregation procedure, adds useful qualitative evidence for long-video operation and another application, and qualifies novelty against concurrent work. These are meaningful but limited gains: the main quantitative evidence is unchanged, and the new demonstrations do not provide systematic validation across prompts or long videos.
